headline: Often called “fake English”, サラリーマン may be real English with a letter dropped.

sources.quote: First cited to 1924 in the novel Chijin no Ai (published in English as Naomi) by Jun’ichirō Tanizaki.

Although often described as wasei eigo (和製英語), this appears to derive from the English phrase salaried man, which appears in print at least as early as 1828. Additionally, the English noun phrase “salary man” also predates the Japanese term. The resulting Japanese term was reimported into English as a compound in the late 20th century.
The form is a regular phonological clipping of the borrowed phrase, dropping the English past‐participle suffix to fit Japanese phonotactics, analyzable as サラリー (sararī) + マン (-man).

The term began to be used in the Taishō period and became firmly established by the early Shōwa period. Prior to its popularization, terms such as 月給取り, 俸給生活者, and 勤め人 were used for similar workers, alongside more derogatory terms like 腰弁当 and 洋服細民. Around 1960, the term ビジネスマン (bijinesuman) also started being used to avoid the mediocre image associated with this word.

examples.ja: 彼は普通のサラリーマンだ。
examples.en: He's just an ordinary office worker.

examples.ja: なあに、しがないサラリーマンですよ。
examples.en: Me? I'm a plain old salaryman.

headline: めがね was “eye metal” first; the kanji came from Chinese later.

sources.quote: Probably originally a compound of 目 (me, “eye”) + 金 (kane, “metal”, in reference to the metal used in eyeglass frames). The kane changes to gane as an instance of rendaku (連濁). The spelling is based on an apparent borrowing from Chinese, see the gankyō reading below.
Appears in texts from the late 1500s.

headline: The kanji say “soil” and “produce”; the likely origin is a shrine's “small box”.

sources.quote: Probably a compound of 宮 (miya, “shrine”) + 笥 (ke, “small box”).
The ke changes to ge as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

examples.ja: これは友人への土産です。
examples.en: These are gifts for my friends.

examples.ja: 旅行から帰るときの土産のことを考えておきなさい。
examples.en: Make allowance for souvenirs on the return trip.

headline: いなか began as “winaka”, and its kanji came from a Chinese word.

sources.quote: /winaka/ → /inaka/
Possibly a compound of 居 (i, the 未然形 (mizenkei, “incomplete form”) and 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem form”) of verb 居る (iru), “to be, exist (of animate objects)”) + 中 (naka, “inside, middle”).
The spelling is from Chinese 田舍 (tiánshè).

examples.ja: 彼女はいなかに住んでいる。
私の家はいなかにあります。
examples.en: My home is in the country.

headline: Brothers have two readings, and they come from two waves of Chinese.

sources.quote: From 兄 (kyō, “elder brother”, goon) + 弟 (dai, “younger brother”, goon), from Middle Chinese 兄弟.

examples.en: My father is one of five brothers.

headline: Soy sauce is “thick paste + oil”, and its sound has smoothed from /ɕauju/ to /ɕoːju/.

sources.quote: /ɕauju/ → /ɕɔːju/ → /ɕoːju/
First attested in the mid-Muromachi period.
Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 醬油 /酱油 (literally “thick paste + oil”).

headline: Buckwheat noodles carry a word whose root may be a “corner” — or a “feather”.

sources.quote: Not attested until the middle of the Muromachi period (1336–1573), as a shortening of older 蕎麦 (soba mugi, literally “soba grain”).
Two theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation of the soba element:
* Samuel Martin reconstructs soba as Proto-Japonic *sonpa and derives it as a compound of *so (unknown) + *pa (“feather”). The *pa changes to *ⁿba as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
* From 稜 (soba, “an edge, a corner”), in reference to the seed of the plant being a triangular oval shape with protruding corners.
Considering the late appearance of soba in isolation with the meaning of buckwheat, and the attested earlier senses of side; corner, edge, Martin's reconstruction seems unlikely.
The kanji spelling is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from 蕎 (“buckwheat”) + 麦 (“wheat”).

examples.ja: すぐそこでそばを立ち食いしてきた。
examples.en: I had a bowl of noodles at a street nearby.

examples.ja: 長野にいる友人を訪問した際、おいしいそばをごちそうになった。
examples.en: When I visited my friend in Nagano, I was treated to delicious soba.
furigana: 、おいしいそばをごちそうになった。

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: A Japanese-made word, built from Chinese parts, to name the telephone.

sources.quote: Wasei kango, created as a translation of English telephone. Coined in Japanese as a compound of Chinese-derived 電 (den, “electric”) + 話 (wa, “talking”). See also 話す (hanasu, “to talk, to chat”).
First attested in a text from 1891.

headline: “Friend” is built as “friends”: an old plural that took over the singular.

sources.quote: From 友(とも) (tomo, “friend”) + 達(たち) (-tachi, pluralizing suffix). Originally plural, but also used in the singular sense in modern Japanese.

examples.en: A friend of mine is coming this evening.

headline: Hand + paper gives “letter” in Japanese, but the identical characters in Chinese are an unrelated false friend.

sources.quote: Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) + 紙 (kami, “paper”). The kami changes to gami as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
An etymologically unrelated false friend of Chinese 手紙 /手纸 (shǒuzhǐ).

headline: Japanese パン is Portuguese pão, and behind that, Latin pānis.

sources.quote: From Portuguese pão (“bread”), from Latin pānem, accusative singular form of pānis (“bread”). Compare French pain, Italian pane, Romanian pâine, Spanish pan.

headline: The spelling you know isn't the original, and the sources disagree about why it works.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 土圭 (tʰuo^X kwei, literally “earth, clay + stack of clay tablets”, a kind of sundial used in the Zhou Dynasty).

The 土圭 spelling is the original form, with the kan'on reading of tokei. This has been largely superseded by the spelling 時計 in modern writing, which uses the 時 character as ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)). Probably this spelling from native Japanese word ときはかり(see below). Alternatively, the kanji spelling could be interpreted as jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), using the meanings of the characters as 時 (“time”) + 計 (“measurement”).

examples.ja: 教会の塔の時計が９時を打った。
examples.en: The clock in the church tower struck nine.

examples.ja: 私のとけいは時間が正確ではありません。
examples.en: My watch doesn't keep good time.

headline: 新しい was once “aratashi”: two syllables swapped places about a thousand years ago.

sources.quote: /arataɕi/ → /ataraɕi/ → /ataraɕiki/ → /ataraɕiː/

In Old Japanese, the original term was 新たし (aratashi), composed of older 新た (arata, “new”) + adjective-forming suffix し (shi). This persisted until at least the mid-1200s, and indeed the adjective stem arata is both modern adjective 新た (arata, -na adjective) and the root of verbs such as 改める (aratameru, “to renew, refresh, revise, or reform something”). See 新た (arata) for further details of that etymology.

Starting from the 900s, the aratashi reading began shifting to atarashi. This metathesis may have been due to conflation with 可惜し (atarashi, “magnificent, excellent, precious; regrettable”). The aratashi reading then became more and more uncommon in Early Middle Japanese, and the “new, modern, fresh” sense became the main use, superseding the largely homophonous 可惜し (atarashi) and pushing it out of common usage.

The modern form is from Early Middle Japanese adjective 新(あたら)し (atarashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in しき (shiki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of しい (shii).
Displaced Old Japanese 新し (nipisi, adjective). This is reflected in the modern language as prefixing stem 新 (nii-), which is no longer productive.

examples.en: His ideas are up to date.

headline: “Stuck flesh”: nobody is sure why a verb for sticking names sliced fish.

sources.quote: Compound of 刺(さ)し (sashi, “sticking into, sticking between; slicing”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 刺(さ)す (sasu, “to stick into”)) + 身(み) (mi, “flesh, meat”). The use of the verb 刺(さ)す (sasu) here to mean slice is irregular, and may be due to the kill connotations of the verb 切(き)る (kiru, “to cut, to slice”) during the Muromachi period when the word sashimi first appears.

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: The Japanese word for a part-time job is German.

sources.quote: Borrowed from German Arbeit (“work, job”).

headline: A teacher is, literally, someone “born earlier”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 先生 (MC sen sraeng, literally “born earlier”).

headline: “Tomorrow” was originally “next morning”, and the kanji came afterwards.

sources.quote: Shift in meaning from 朝 (ashita, “next morning”), itself cognate with 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The kanji spelling is from Chinese 明日 (míngrì).

examples.en: I wonder if he'll come tomorrow.

headline: It sounds like English “consent” but it is “concentric plug”, shortened.

sources.quote: Clipping of コンセントリックプラグ (konsentorikku puragu), wasei eigo (和製英語; pseudo-anglicism) derived from concentric + plug, used since the late Meiji period. Sometimes the source word is mistaken for the unrelated English consent, which would be transliterated the same way.

examples.ja: 彼はラジオをコンセントにつないだ。
furigana: はラジオをコンセントにつないだ。

headline: “Go out” + “mouth”: an exit is a door with a voiced mouth.

sources.quote: 出(で)る (deru, “to exit”) + 口(くち) (kuchi, “opening, door”).
The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

examples.ja: 彼らは出口のほうに進んだ。

headline: “Thank you” started out meaning “hard to exist”, which is to say, rare.

sources.quote: Phonetic shift: /ariɡataku/ → /ariɡatau/ → /ariɡatoː/.

From ありがたく (arigataku), the adverbial form of Old Japanese and Classical Japanese adjective ありがたし (arigatashi, modern ありがたい arigatai, “grateful, thankful; welcome”), from 有り (ari, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, continuative or stem form) of verb 有る aru, “to exist, to be”) + 難し (katashi, “hard, difficult”, 難い katai in modern Japanese). The katashi changes to gatashi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

Modern Japanese -i adjectives formerly ended in -ki for the attributive form. This medial /k/ dropped out during the Muromachi period, both for the attributive form (-ki becoming -i) and for the adverbial form (-ku becoming -u). However, the adverbial form reverted to -ku thereafter for most words, with the -u ending persisting in certain everyday set expressions, such as arigatō, おはよう (ohayō), or おめでとう (omedetō), and in hyper-formal speech.

Arigatashi is first attested in the oldest literature of the 8th century. It originally meant “difficult to exist, hard to be”, shifting to “rare, special”, and then to “welcome, thankful, nice to have” by some time in the 15th century. This sense is still in use:
: この天(てん)気(き)はありがたいね。 ― Kono tenki wa arigatai ne. ― This weather sure is welcome (literally, “This weather sure is hard to come by”)
The similarity to Portuguese obrigado (“thank you”) is purely coincidental; the Portuguese first arrived in Japan in 1543, well over a century after citations expressing gratitude are found.

headline: Fruit is literally “tree's thing”, with a lost possessive hiding in the middle.

sources.quote: Literally “tree's thing”. Originally a compound of 木 (ku, “tree”, irregular shift from ancient ko pronunciation) + だ (da, possessive marker between two nouns, only found in a few compounds) + 物 (mono, “thing”).
The medial da is also seen in 獣 (kedamono, “beast”, literally “hairy thing”). The kanji is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

examples.ja: レモンはすっぱいくだものだ。
examples.en: The lemon is a sour fruit.

examples.ja: どんなくだものがご入用ですか。
examples.en: What kind of fruit do you want?

headline: Typhoon is a borrowing that was later dressed in Chinese-looking kanji.

sources.quote: First attested in Japanese in 1900 in the katakana form タイフーン (taifūn), itself a borrowing from English typhoon.

Prior to the Meiji era (1868–1912), this kind of severe storm was called a 野分き (nowaki), literally a "field-splitter" for the way the winds would wreak havoc on farms. The term タイフーン (taifūn) then appears in 1900, also attested with spelling 大風 and reading of taifun. Then in 1907 meteorologist Okada Takematsu (岡田武松) scientifically defined what qualifies as this specific type of storm, and then purportedly as phono-semantic matching of the English typhoon, adopted the kyūjitai kanji spelling 颱風 (read as taifū without that final "n") on the basis of Chinese references using the term 颱風 /台风 (táifēng). This spelling then became common from the Taisho era (1912–1926).

There was likely some influence from Chinese on the form of the Japanese word. In Walter Henry Medhurst's English and Chinese Dictionary of 1847-48, he glossed the English word typhoon as Chinese 太風 /太风 and 颶風 /飓风 (jùfēng), the former of which would be read in Japanese as taifū.
The origins of English typhoon are somewhat uncertain, with possible ancient connections to Chinese. See that entry for more.
台 is a daiyōji replacing 颱.

examples.en: The typhoon caused the river to flood.

headline: A tatami is, at heart, something you fold.

sources.quote: From 畳む (tatamu, “to fold”, verb).

examples.ja: 彼は畳の上に大の字になった。
examples.en: He lay on the mat at full length.

examples.ja: 畳に座っていたので足が痛い。
examples.en: My legs ache from sitting on tatami.

headline: Delicious began as an honorific: “o-” + “ishii”.

sources.quote: Originally from 御 (o-, honorific prefix) + 美しい (ishii, “good; delicious”, possibly obsolete in modern contexts; the delicious sense evolved out of 女房詞 (nyōbo kotoba, “women's word”) usage).

headline: ゆかた is the front half of a longer word, and the kanji say “bathing garment”.

sources.quote: Clipping of 湯帷子 (yukatabira).

headline: Nobody knows where たのしい comes from, and all three theories have problems.

sources.quote: ⟨tano₁siki₁⟩ → */tanʷosikʲi/ → /tanoshii/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. No Ryukyuan cognates exist; as a result, further derivation unknown. Theories include:
* A compound of 手 (ta, “hand”, combining form) + 伸す (nosu, “to extend”)
*: This is problematic, as nosu has first been attested starting from the early 900s, with no A/B distinction (see Jōdai Tokushu Kanazukai for details).
* From 田神 (tano, literally “rice paddy god”)
*: No reading of 神 (*no, “god”) exists.
* A borrowing from an unknown language
*: No words resemble *tanV meaning "fun" or "to enjoy".

headline: A kimono was once just “a wearing-thing”: any clothing at all.

sources.quote: Compound of 着(き) (ki, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 着(き)る (kiru, “to wear clothing”)) + 物(もの) (-mono, “thing”). Compare the similar formation of the word 食(た)べ物(もの) (tabemono, “food”, literally “eating thing”).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE in the ideographic spelling 裳, later attested less ambiguously in the Utsubo Monogatari of the late 900s CE.

As contact with the West grew, the sense shifted from referring generically to any clothing to referring specifically to 和服(わふく) (wafuku, “(traditional) Japanese clothing”), in particular kimono and other robe-like full-length garments (長着(ながぎ) (nagagi)), as opposed to Western apparel (洋服(ようふく) (yōfuku)).

examples.ja: なかなか「きもの」を着る機会がないというかたも、思い切って着てみましょう！
examples.en: Also, those of you who don't have the chance to wear a 'kimono', go for it and wear one!
furigana: がないというかたも、思い切って

headline: A “self-rolling vehicle”, coined in Japan in 1870 for a tricycle.

sources.quote: Coined in Japan in 1870 in the Meiji period in reference to a patented tricycle design. Later used to refer to bicycles.
Compound of Sinitic-derived elements 自 (ji, “self”) + 転 (ten, “rolling”, simplified modern form of 轉) + 車 (sha, “vehicle”).

headline: A fire was once “the matter of fire”, a native phrase later re-read in Chinese sounds.

sources.quote: Old Japanese 火事 (pi₂ no₂ ko₂to₂) (now spelled as 火の事 (hi no koto)), later read with 音読み (on'yomi).

examples.en: We often have fires in winter.

headline: “Dream” began as “sleep-eye”: sight seen while asleep.

sources.quote: ⟨i me₂⟩ → */jiməɨ/ → /jɨme/ → /jume/
Shift from Old Japanese 夢 (ime₂), itself a compound of 寝 (i, “sleep, sleeping”, obsolete) + 目 (me, “eye; sight, vision”).
Appears in texts from the 900s.

examples.en: It's like a dream come true.

headline: けしき was spelled another way first; 景 was swapped in for the sense.

sources.quote: Derived from 気(け)色(しき) (keshiki).
